newsitem.title: UK: British "debs" ball shows old rituals live on.
newsitem.headline: British "debs" ball shows old rituals live on.

text.p: Young women from Britain's richest and aristocratic families will make their social debut before royalty on Monday in an old ritual which has survived the increasing egalitarianism of late 20th century society.

The debs, average age around 18, will saunter down the grand staircase at the "Great House" in London's prestigious Grosvenor House and curtsy in front of the Duke of Kent, the Queen's cousin -- a ceremony which symbolises acceptance at court.
Then vintage champagne will flow as 500 of Britain's wealthy elite dance the night away at Queen Charlotte's Birthday Ball, named over 200 years ago after the wife of King George III.

The "presentation at court" of debutantes -- daughters of the nation's rich and titled -- has been a tradition for centuries. But "coming out" as a passport into high society only took hold during the reign of Queen Victoria in the mid-19th century.
Securing a presentation was a positive step to social advancement as well as a way of showing loyalty to the monarch.
After World War Two, however, the idea of "society', in its pre-war sense seemed increasingly outmoded. The last "debs" were presented to Queen Elizabeth in 1958.

Monday's presentation will not involve the queen and will be held in a London hotel instead of Buckingham Palace. But the atmosphere will still reflect a more gracious age, according to the ball's organisers.
Proceeds from the 125-pound ($195) a head party go to the Queen Charlotte hospital in London.
"Obviously it is a very glamorous social event but support for the hospital is in the forefront," the blue-blooded event's chairwoman, the Countess of St Andrews, told Reuters.
The Countess was speaking on Wednesday at an auction at fine art auctioneers Christies, also being held for Queen Charlotte's, Britain oldest maternity hospital.

The auction, which raised just under 15,000 pounds ($23,400), featured such items as a set of crystal wine goblets donated by the Queen Mother and a pair of wooden candlesticks, from her great-grandson, the Viscount Linley.
Proceeds from the auction, the ball and donations on the night should push the total to around 100,000 pounds ($156,000).
The countess dismissed suggestions the money spent on a party for the rich would be better given directly to the charity.
"The fact is these types of parties go on all of the time. We have to come up with an event that people will want to go to."
The debutantes will wear gowns created by Britain's top designers, including Bruce Oldfield, who also supplies Diana, the Princess of Wales.
They bow to the duke beside a huge cake, an act with its roots in the 1780s when George III, the king who went mad, used to throw birthday parties for his wife, Charlotte.
The first Queen Charlotte's Ball was held in 1928. In 1940, Winston Churchill attended while his daughter Mary processed as a deb.

The Countess expects around 40 women to parade before the Duke but said there could be more. "The girls are more nervous about doing this than those of the past. They have to talk each other into it," she said. ($1=.6430 Pound)
